newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook - Shutdowns to absord length.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook - Shutdowns to absord length.

text.p: The ample length in the Asian oil product markets is due to be absorbed by fresh demand arising from refinery shutdowns and the return of Chinese buyers after their New Year celebrations, traders said on Monday.
Fuel oil prices were bolstered last week amid a larger-than-expected purchase from Taiwan of 114,000 tonnes for March arrivals and fresh demand from India and Thailand.
Shutdowns at three Thai refineries in January and early February spurred a fuel oil requirement but stalled all gasoline and diesel exports to tide over the unexpected shortage.

In second half-January, Bangchak Petroleum Plc closed a 40,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) crude unit for a two-week scheduled turnaround in the second half of January while technical problems prompted the Star Petroleum Refinery Co partially shutdown secondary units at its 130,000-bpd refinery for a week.
Similar operational problems closed the Thai Petrochemical Industry's 65,000-bpd condensate splitter for 10 days in early January.
While no February or March gasoline exports are expected, one Thai refiner even emerged to buy a 95-octane gasoline for first-half March arrival, adding further support to an already bullish market.
Traders said the tightness of gasoline barrels in February is likely to roll over to March with India buying 90,000 tonnes of 87-octane unleaded gasoline from one supplier, a Dutch trader.

After its disappointing purchase of only one 250,000-barrel cargo of 95-octane unleaded reformate, Taiwan is expected to buy more than one cargo in its tender for second-half March. The tender closes February 18 and is valid until February 20.

Distillate supplies in March are also expected to tighten with the shutdown of Singapore's Mobil Corp 280,000-bpd refinery for six-weeks from mid-March and Singapore Refining Co's 90,000-bpd crude unit March 2-22. Indonesia's 120,000-bpd Dumai refinery plans next weekend for around one month.
The shutdowns should temper the fall of more than $2.00 per barrel seen in the Singapore jet/kerosene prices last week, traders said.
They said the market began to head south as the second and third quarters are traditionally periods of low demand as north Asian countries stop buying the winter heating fuel.
"Japan and South Korea are not buying any more jet for the winter," a trader at a Japanese trading house said.
Japan, the region's largest importer of jet fuel in winter, has not bought any new cargoes since the beginning of February due to high domestic stocks and a mild winter, the trader said.

Although currently under pressure from an abundance of prompt supplies and aggressive sellers caught out with Mideast cargoes intended for the China market, gas oil rebounded late last week as its fall was capped by the cuts in regional prodution.
Traders said physical gas oil supplies in Singapore had tightened after some prompt supplies were sold for export to the Indian sub-continent totalling 80,000-tonnes and 60,000-tonnes to Thailand.
Traders were also looking for further support from India's import tender for April which closes February 20.

Naphtha buyers were sidelined and expected to maintain their low profile during term talks with Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) held in Singapore February 17. About a dozen trading houses, oil firms and petrochemical end-users from Japan and South Korea are due to discuss contracts for March 1997-April 1998 supplies.
"End-users don't want to give KPC the impression that the market is bullish ahead of the talks," one trader said.
